# Heterosis, dominance, and what divergence buys {#sec-heterosis} Since @sec-subdivided this book has repeated a claim without proving it: that the divergence between the heterotic pools is the engine of heterosis, and is therefore to be maintained rather than minimised. @sec-catalogue will decompose diversity on that basis and @sec-stages will build a monitoring panel around it. The claim has carried a lot of weight for an assertion. This chapter derives it, and then corrects it. The derivation is short and the identity is exact. The correction is that the usual reading of the identity -- *push the pools apart and you will get more heterosis* -- is false: under neutral divergence expected heterosis does not move at all, and the simulation shows it. The chapter then goes one step past the mean. Expected heterosis is what a pool pair is worth on average; what a breeder selects on is how heterosis is *distributed* across the crosses of the factorial. Those are different questions with different answers, and the second one is where general and specific combining ability come from. The derivations come first and @sec-heterosis-protocol turns them into the eight steps that compute them on a real programme's data, with the check and the failure mode of each one. Read that section first if the question is what to run rather than why it holds. Three premises carry everything below. They are stated here once, because every result in the chapter uses all three and two of them are restrictive. **Parents are fully inbred.** Every parent line is homozygous at every locus, so an F1's marker row is the average of its two parents' rows and a locus is heterozygous in the F1 exactly when the parents differ. This is what makes the additive effects cancel from the mid-parent difference and what makes `GD_WI` zero. Note that this is a property of the *programme*, not of the mating system: the crop here is allogamous -- maize-type, two heterotic pools under reciprocal recurrent selection -- and it is DH induction or selfing to fixation that delivers homozygous parents from it. Nothing here transfers to a programme crossing non-inbred parents (an inter-population cross, a synthetic, S1 parents) without re-derivation, and @sec-heterosis-step1 measures how large the error is if the formulae below are applied anyway: a factor of five, not a few per cent. **The genotypic model is dominance within loci and additivity between them.** There is no epistatic term anywhere below: the genotypic value is a sum over loci, $H_i$ is a sum of per-locus indicators, and the combining-ability expansion of @sec-heterosis-gca-sca is bilinear only because no term couples two loci. @labroo2021 review epistasis alongside dominance as a proposed mechanism for heterosis; this model excludes it, and no result below should be read as evidence about it. What $d_k$ does absorb is every *within-locus* story, as the next section sets out. **The marker panel is the set of dominance loci.** $d_k$ is indexed by the same $k$ as the markers, so every locus carrying dominance is genotyped and the frequency statistics are computed on exactly the loci that generate heterosis. This is the strongest assumption of the three, and it is the one that carries the distance results of @sec-heterosis-distance. A real panel tags causal loci through linkage disequilibrium rather than containing them, which weakens every statement below about markers predicting heterosis but does not change the algebra, since the algebra is written over whatever set $k$ indexes. ## The dominance model, minimally ### The one-locus scale The classical parameterisation puts the origin at the midpoint of the two homozygotes: one homozygote is worth $+a$, the other $-a$, and the heterozygote $d$. Under random mating at frequency $p$, with $q = 1 - p$, the population mean is [@falconer1996, Eq. 7.2] $$M = a\,(p - q) + 2pq\,d$$ The first term is the additive contribution, and the mid-parent of any cross already carries it. The second is the dominance contribution. It is the only part of $M$ that depends on how many heterozygotes there are, and therefore the only part a cross can add over its own mid-parent. ::: {.callout-note} ## $a$ is a scale, not a quantity this chapter computes The symbols in that display are the textbook ones. This book's additive marker effects are $\beta_k$ (@sec-genomic-prediction), and its $\alpha$ is the diversity-loss statistic of @sec-catalogue, not the classical average effect of a substitution. The per-locus $a_k$ reappears three times below and never as a result: in the genotypic-value model used to show that it cancels, in the definition of overdominance as $|d| > |a|$, and in the average effect of a substitution $a + d(q - p)$. No quantity this chapter reports depends on it. ::: ### What $d_k$ is, and what it is not $d_k$ is *functional* dominance: the departure of the heterozygote from the homozygote midpoint at locus $k$. It is a property of the locus. It does not move when allele frequencies move. Fisher's *statistical* dominance deviation is a different object: the residual left after projecting genotypic values onto the best additive model **in a particular population**. It is a property of the population as much as of the locus, and it changes when frequencies change. Both appear in this chapter, and keeping them apart is the whole trick. $d_k$ is the input. The specific combining ability of @sec-heterosis-gca-sca is the statistical dominance deviation that a given $d_k$ *induces* over a given pair of pools. One is a constant; the other is an answer that depends on where the pools happen to sit. The distinction also buys the model what generality it has, and marks where that generality stops. Dominance, overdominance (a heterozygote outside both homozygotes, $|d| > |a|$) and pseudo-overdominance (two dominant favourable alleles in repulsion phase, too close for any marker to separate) are three different biological stories, and @labroo2021 review the evidence for each. At marker resolution they are the same arithmetic: a locus at which the F1 gains something the mid-parent does not. A single $d_k$ absorbs all three, and nothing below can distinguish them -- nor needs to. Epistasis is the fourth story on @labroo2021's list and $d_k$ does not absorb it, because a single per-locus number cannot represent a term that depends on two loci at once. That is the second premise above, and it is an exclusion rather than an approximation. ### The mid-parent difference Code a genotype by $x_k \in \{0, 0.5, 1\}$, the frequency of the reference allele within the individual, and take the genotypic value to be the additive part plus the dominance deviation at every heterozygous locus: $$G(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_k a_k\,(2x_k - 1) + \sum_k d_k\,\mathbb{1}\{x_k = 0.5\}$$ The parents are fully inbred, so each is homozygous at every locus and the F1's row is the average of its two parents' rows. The additive part is linear in $\mathbf{x}$, so the two parents' additive values average exactly to the F1's own and cancel from the mid-parent difference. What survives is the dominance deviation at the loci where the F1 is heterozygous: $$H_i = \sum_k d_k \, \mathbb{1}\{x_{ik} = 0.5\}$$ The additive effects never appear. That is the result, not an omission, and it is why `heterosis_value()` takes no additive-effect argument: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} heterosis_value #> function (X, d) #> { #> stopifnot(length(d) == ncol(X)) #> drop((X == 0.5) %*% d) #> } #> #> ``` ::: Against the literal oracle of @sec-verification, which loops over loci and compares the two parents' genotypes one at a time: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} max(abs(heterosis_value(ctx$X[1:25, ], d) - ref_heterosis(L, head(ctx$ped, 25), d))) #> [1] 0 ``` ::: The cancellation is worth seeing directly. Draw additive effects at random, score a real F1 and its two parents under $G(\mathbf{x})$, and subtract: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(9) # the cancellation is exact for any a; seed it anyway a <- rnorm(ctx$m, 0, 0.2) val <- function(x) sum(a * (2 * x - 1)) + sum(d * (x == 0.5)) i <- 7 mid <- (val(L[ctx$ped$a[i], ] / 2) + val(L[ctx$ped$b[i], ] / 2)) / 2 c(mid_parent_difference = val(ctx$X[i, ]) - mid, heterosis_value = heterosis_value(ctx$X[i, , drop = FALSE], d)) #> mid_parent_difference heterosis_value #> 362.3386 362.3386 ``` ::: The additive effects entered the first number and cancelled out of it; they never entered the second. ## Expected heterosis over a pool pair Write $p_{Ak}$ and $p_{Bk}$ for the reference-allele frequencies at locus $k$ in the two pools, each computed over that pool's lines. A locus is heterozygous in the F1 when the two gametes carry different alleles, which for a cross drawn at random between the pools happens with probability $p_A(1 - p_B) + (1 - p_A)p_B$. The expected heterosis over all $A \times B$ crosses therefore follows from the pool frequencies alone: $$\mathbb{E}[H] = \sum_k d_k \left[\, p_{A k} + p_{B k} - 2 p_{A k} p_{B k} \right]$$ The candidate pool here *is* the full factorial, every $A \times B$ pairing exactly once, and the frequencies are the means of those same lines. The closed form is then the mean of the realised values as an identity rather than an approximation, and the residual is at machine precision: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} abs(heterosis_expected(pA, pB, d) - mean(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d))) #> [1] 1.136868e-13 ``` ::: That is a mean over $N =$ 625 crosses, and a mean is not a ranking. Hold on to the question of how the individual crosses are spread around it; @sec-heterosis-gca-sca answers it exactly. ## The identity {#sec-heterosis-identity} Now split the bracket. Writing $\bar p = (p_A + p_B)/2$ and $y = p_A - p_B$, the per-locus F1 heterozygosity separates exactly: $$p_A + p_B - 2 p_A p_B \;=\; \underbrace{2 \bar p (1 - \bar p)}_{\text{shared}} \;+\; \underbrace{y^2 / 2}_{\text{divergence}}$$ The first term is the heterozygosity a single merged pool at frequency $\bar p$ would produce under random mating. The second is what keeping the pools apart adds on top of it. Average both over loci with $d_k \equiv 1$, so that the weighting does not obscure the algebra, and they are exactly the $GD_T$ and $GD_{BS}$ of the Caballero & Toro partition that @sec-subdivided derived and `gd_partition()` computes: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hp <- heterosis_partition(pA, pB, rep(1, ctx$m)) / ctx$m gp <- gd_partition(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx) fmt(data.frame(term = c("shared", "divergence"), heterosis = c(hp[["shared"]], hp[["divergence"]]), partition = c(gp[["GD_T"]], gp[["GD_BS"]]), residual = c(abs(hp[["shared"]] - gp[["GD_T"]]), abs(hp[["divergence"]] - gp[["GD_BS"]]))), 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | heterosis| partition| residual| |:----------|---------:|---------:|--------:| |shared | 0.3280928| 0.3280928| 0| |divergence | 0.0335968| 0.0335968| 0|
::: ::: > $GD_{BS}$ weighted by dominance deviations **is** the divergence half of expected > heterosis. "Between-pool divergence is the heterosis engine" is an identity, not > a slogan. One thing to be clear about before reading on. $GD_T$ is the gene diversity of the *merged* population, and by @sec-subdivided it already contains $GD_{BS}$: with inbred lines, $GD_T = GD_{BI} + GD_{BS}$. Expected F1 heterozygosity is therefore $GD_{BI} + 2\,GD_{BS}$, the between-pool component counted twice -- once inside the shared term, once as the divergence term. That factor of two is where the classical result sits. Falconer & Mackay's heterosis of a cross between two *random-mating* populations is $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$ [@falconer1996, Ch. 14], exactly twice the divergence term here. The two do not conflict; they use different mid-parents. Theirs is two random-mating populations, each carrying its own within-pool heterozygosity, so their $H$ is the total above $\sum_k d_k (p_{Ak}q_{Ak} + p_{Bk}q_{Bk})$. Ours is two inbred lines carrying none, so the whole F1 heterozygosity is heterosis, and the shared term is the mean of the two pools' random-mating heterozygosities plus the half of $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$ that $GD_T$ already holds. That paragraph is an algebraic claim and it can be checked rather than asserted. Subtract the random-mating mid-parent from the F1's total dominance value and what is left is $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$, exactly twice this chapter's divergence term: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hpd <- heterosis_partition(pA, pB, d) mid_random_mating <- sum(d * (pA * (1 - pA) + pB * (1 - pB))) stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(hpd[["total"]] - mid_random_mating, 2 * hpd[["divergence"]])), isTRUE(all.equal(2 * hpd[["divergence"]], sum(d * (pA - pB)^2)))) c(F1_total = hpd[["total"]], mid_random_mating = mid_random_mating, difference = hpd[["total"]] - mid_random_mating, twice_divergence = 2 * hpd[["divergence"]], sum_d_y2 = sum(d * (pA - pB)^2)) #> F1_total mid_random_mating difference twice_divergence #> 355.66859 289.77816 65.89042 65.89042 #> sum_d_y2 #> 65.89042 ``` ::: The first number is what an F1 between two inbred lines gains over *its* mid-parent of zero; the third is what the same F1 gains over a mid-parent of two random-mating pools. They differ by 289.8 units of dominance value that the random-mating parents already carry themselves. Which mid-parent is the right one is not a matter of convention: it is whichever one the programme actually plants. @sec-heterosis-step1 measures the consequence of getting it wrong. ### A third form: one minus the between-pool coancestry The sum of the two components has a name of its own. $\theta_{AB} = \mathbf{w}_A' \mathbf{f}^L \mathbf{w}_B$ is the between-pool coancestry of @sec-catalogue: on the full factorial, where the line weights are uniform, it is the probability that an allele drawn from a pool-A line and an allele drawn from a pool-B line are identical in state. Its complement is the whole bracket: $$GD_T + GD_{BS} \;=\; 1 - \theta_{AB}$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tp <- theta_pools(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx) c(shared_plus_divergence = gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]], one_minus_theta_AB = 1 - tp[["theta_AB"]]) #> shared_plus_divergence one_minus_theta_AB #> 0.3616896 0.3616896 ``` ::: This one is algebra rather than simulation. `gd_partition()` defines $GD_T = 1 - \bar f$ and $GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f$ with $\bar f = (\theta_A + 2\theta_{AB} + \theta_B)/4$ and $\tilde f = (\theta_A + \theta_B)/2$, and the sum collapses to $1 - \theta_{AB}$. Which is the shortest statement the chapter has to make: **expected F1 heterozygosity is one minus between-pool coancestry.** Everything else here is a weighting of that quantity, or a way of splitting it. ## A second identity, at the hybrid level @sec-catalogue reports `GD_WI_hyb`, the within-individual gene diversity actually carried by the F1s, separately from the line-level partition, because with inbred parents `GD_WI` is zero by construction and carries no signal. A hybrid's self-coancestry is $1 - h_i/2$, with $h_i$ its heterozygous fraction, so `GD_WI_hyb` is half the mean F1 heterozygosity and the two levels are linked: $$2 \cdot GD_{WI\text{-}hyb} = GD_T + GD_{BS}$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c(lhs = 2 * gp[["GD_WI_hyb"]], rhs = gp[["GD_T"]] + gp[["GD_BS"]], GD_WI = gp[["GD_WI"]]) #> lhs rhs GD_WI #> 3.616896e-01 3.616896e-01 -4.440892e-16 ``` ::: Exact on the full factorial, because every $A \times B$ pairing is present exactly once. On a *selected* subset it holds only approximately. There $GD_T$ and $GD_{BS}$ are computed from the line-usage weights, which is what a random re-pairing of the selected parents would give, while `GD_WI_hyb` scores the pairs actually chosen. The gap is the pairing structure of the subset. `tests/testthat/test-dominance.R` asserts the identity to `1e-12` on the full factorial and, on a *random* 40-hybrid subset at one scale (12 lines per pool, 800 markers), bounds the gap with `expect_equal(tolerance = 5e-3)`. That tolerance is **relative**, not absolute: on a gene-diversity value of order 0.4 the absolute bound it enforces is of order `2e-3`, and the gap the test actually sees is smaller again. A subset chosen by an optimiser, which concentrates line usage deliberately, is not covered by that bound; @sec-era-fhom is where it is measured, on four such subsets at this book's scale, and reports the largest departure of the four. ## Inbreeding depression, and why it does not price $\alpha$ {#sec-heterosis-id} The same model run backwards gives inbreeding depression. A locus at frequency $p$ in a population with inbreeding coefficient $F$ is heterozygous with probability $2pq(1-F)$, so the mean declines linearly in $F$ [@falconer1996, Ch. 14]: $$ID \;=\; 2F\sum_k d_k \, p_k q_k$$ At $F = 1$ that is exactly the *shared* term of `heterosis_partition()` evaluated at $p_A = p_B = p$. So the depression of a pool driven to complete homozygosity and the expected heterosis of a cross made *within* that same pool are one quantity seen from two sides. @mackay2020 treat heterosis and inbreeding depression together on that basis, alongside transgressive segregation, which this chapter does not take up. The identity needs no new machinery: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c(inbreeding_depression = inbreeding_depression(pA, d), shared_term = heterosis_partition(pA, pA, d)[["shared"]], deviation = abs(inbreeding_depression(pA, d) - heterosis_partition(pA, pA, d)[["shared"]])) #> inbreeding_depression shared_term deviation #> 288.2869 288.2869 0.0000 ``` ::: The closed form is checked against simulated genotypes rather than against its own algebra, which is what `ref_inbreeding_depression()` exists for: it draws each genotype as identical by descent with probability $F$ and as two independent alleles otherwise, so the agreement is to Monte Carlo error: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} k <- 1:300 c(closed_form = inbreeding_depression(pA[k], d[k], 0.6), simulated = ref_inbreeding_depression(pA[k], d[k], 0.6, n = 20000, seed = 2)) #> closed_form simulated #> 27.58563 27.57923 ``` ::: Now the part that matters, because the obvious next step is wrong. It is tempting to argue: $\alpha$ budgets a loss of within-pool gene diversity; gene diversity is $\sum_k p_kq_k$; inbreeding depression is $\sum_k d_k\,p_kq_k$; therefore spending $\alpha$ costs yield in the current cycle, and *that* is the price of the budget. The algebra does not support it. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c(max_dominance_contribution_of_an_inbred_line = max(abs(heterosis_value(U, d)))) #> max_dominance_contribution_of_an_inbred_line #> 0 ``` ::: Zero, exactly. A fully inbred line has no heterozygous loci, so its dominance contribution is zero **whatever the pool's allele frequencies are**. In a programme whose parents are inbred lines the depression was paid in full when the lines were made; it is a constant, and it does not move when the pool subsequently loses diversity. The formula above describes the gap between a hypothetical random-mating pool and its inbred derivatives, and that gap *shrinks* as $p_kq_k$ shrinks -- but nothing in the programme stands at the random-mating end of it. ::: {.callout-important} ## Inbreeding depression is not the current-cycle price of the diversity budget This is the same fact that makes $GD_{WI}$ exactly zero in @sec-catalogue's partition, and it has the same cause: with inbred parents there is no within-individual variation left to lose. Two consequences. The cost of $\alpha$ in this system remains what @sec-cycles measures -- an option value, realised cycles later through the variance available to select on (@sec-response), not a yield loss booked this season. And inbreeding depression **is** the live quantity wherever the population is only partially inbred: F2, F3 and F4 in @sec-sizing, where $F$ is still climbing and the depression is still accumulating. That is the chapter it belongs to, not this one. ::: Note also what this does *not* say. Expected heterosis in the product is a separate question. @sec-heterosis-flat answers it for the neutral case: under drift the shared term lost and the divergence term gained cancel exactly, so hybrid heterosis is invariant. Under selection the frequencies move directionally, and what happens to expected heterosis is then the alignment question of @sec-heterosis-alignment, which can go either way. In neither case is the diversity loss itself an immediate dominance cost. The bill arrives later, and it arrives in the additive variance. ## When genetic distance predicts heterosis exactly {#sec-heterosis-distance} Before the corrections start, one special case is worth having, because it is the only case in which marker distance and heterosis are the same number. Set $d_k \equiv d$, constant across loci. Then $H$ stops being a weighted count and becomes a plain one: $d$ times the number of loci at which the two parents differ. For inbred lines that count is exactly what the coancestry kernel of @sec-coancestry measures, so for a cross between lines $a$ and $b$ $$H_{ab} \;=\; d\,m\,(1 - f^L_{ab}) \;=\; d\,m\,\mathrm{MRD}_{ab}^2$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} h1 <- heterosis_value(ctx$X, rep(1, ctx$m)) fL <- molecular_coancestry(L / 2) ab <- cbind(ctx$ped$a, ctx$ped$b) c(vs_coancestry = max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * (1 - fL[ab]))), vs_mrd = max(abs(h1 - ctx$m * mrd_matrix(L / 2)[ab]^2))) #> vs_coancestry vs_mrd #> 1.136868e-13 2.273737e-13 ``` ::: Both residuals are at machine precision. Under flat dominance, heterosis and molecular coancestry are one statistic seen twice -- Trap 1 of @sec-stages read from the other side -- and the diversity kernel this whole book runs on turns out to be the right object for the heterosis question as well. Flat $d$ is also precisely the condition under which $H$ is a function of marker distance alone. It is a strong condition, and it fails as soon as $d$ varies: two crosses at the same distance then differ by *which* loci they differ at. With the gamma-distributed deviations used everywhere else in this chapter the relationship survives but stops being an identity: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c(cor_uniform_d = cor(h1, 1 - fL[ab]), cor_real_d = cor(heterosis_value(ctx$X, d), 1 - fL[ab])) #> cor_uniform_d cor_real_d #> 1.0000000 0.7809147 ``` ::: A correlation of 0.78 is a useful predictor and a poor identity. Two things move it, and both are properties of the germplasm rather than of the statistic: how $d$ is spread over the loci at which the parents differ, which is what @sec-heterosis-alignment is about, and -- once the third premise is relaxed -- how well the panel tags the causal loci. Under flat $d$ on a panel that *is* the causal set the correlation is 1 by the identity above. Departing from either condition generally lowers it -- not always, since a $d$ that varies only across loci at which no pair of parents differs changes no $H_i$ at all -- and by how much is something this chapter does not attempt to predict. ## Divergence is not a bonus {#sec-heterosis-flat} Read `divergence` as free money and you will reach for $F_{ST}$. Do not. Draw the pools further apart and watch all three terms. Nothing here is selected. Each point re-draws both pools from the *same* ancestral frequencies -- the ancestral vector is fixed by `seed = 5` and shared across the sweep, while the two pool-frequency vectors are fresh Balding-Nichols draws at each `fst` (@sec-notation) -- so what varies along the sweep is how far the draw scatters and nothing else: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sweep_het <- function(fst) { cf <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, seed = 5)) Lf <- simulate_lines(cf) pl <- rep(c("A", "B"), c(cf$n_pool_A, cf$n_pool_B)) Pf <- pool_freqs(Lf / 2, pl) hp <- heterosis_partition(Pf["A", ], Pf["B", ], rep(1, cf$m)) / cf$m cm <- pool_complementarity(Lf / 2, pl) data.frame(fst = fst, shared = hp[["shared"]], divergence = hp[["divergence"]], total = hp[["total"]], frac_opposite_fixed = cm[["frac_opposite_fixed"]], mean_abs_delta_p = cm[["mean_abs_delta_p"]], mean_sq_delta_p = cm[["mean_sq_delta_p"]]) } sw <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45), sweep_het)) # Read again in @sec-heterosis-step5: no marker is fixed for opposite alleles # anywhere below fst = 0.20, while the divergence term has already more than # doubled over that span. stopifnot(all(sw$frac_opposite_fixed[sw$fst <= 0.10] == 0)) fmt(sw, 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

::: ::: Across the sweep the divergence term rises by a factor of 7.9. The comparison that matters is in absolute units, not in ratios: divergence gains 0.0739 per locus and the shared term loses 0.0756. The total does not move. ### The two terms, term by term The algebra is one line. Pool A and pool B are drawn *independently* around a common ancestral frequency $p$, so $\mathbb{E}[p_A] = \mathbb{E}[p_B] = p$ and $\mathbb{E}[p_A p_B] = p^2$. Therefore $$\mathbb{E}\!\left[p_A + p_B - 2 p_A p_B\right] = 2p(1-p),$$ which contains no $F_{ST}$ at all. With ancestral frequencies drawn uniformly on $[0.05, 0.95]$ the predicted level is $\mathbb{E}[2p(1-p)] =$ 0.365, against a simulated mean of 0.3646 across the whole sweep. That the *sum* is flat is the headline, but the Balding-Nichols model predicts each half separately, which is the sharper statement. Under it $\mathrm{Var}(p_A) = \mathrm{Var}(p_B) = F_{ST}\,p(1-p)$, so $\mathrm{Var}(\bar p) = F_{ST}\,p(1-p)/2$ and $\mathrm{Var}(y) = 2F_{ST}\,p(1-p)$. Substituting: $$\mathbb{E}\!\left[2\bar p(1 - \bar p)\right] = 2p(1-p)\left(1 - \tfrac{F_{ST}}{2}\right), \qquad \mathbb{E}\!\left[y^2/2\right] = F_{ST}\,p(1-p)$$ The shared term loses $F_{ST}\,p(1-p)$ and the divergence term gains $F_{ST}\,p(1-p)$: the same expression with opposite signs, not approximately and not on average over some range. Both predictions are parameter-free once the ancestral distribution is fixed, so they can be laid straight on top of the sweep: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} Ep <- 2 * (0.5 - (0.9^2 / 12 + 0.25)) # E[2p(1-p)] for p ~ U(0.05, 0.95) sw$pred_shared <- Ep * (1 - sw$fst / 2) sw$pred_divergence <- Ep * sw$fst / 2 fmt(sw[, c("fst", "shared", "pred_shared", "divergence", "pred_divergence")], 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

Now the spread. The same expansion that produced the shared/divergence split produces the combining-ability decomposition, with no new machinery and no model fitting. Let $u_{ik} \in \{0, 1\}$ be the genotype of pool-A line $i$ at locus $k$ and $v_{jk}$ that of pool-B line $j$, and write each as its pool frequency plus a deviation, $u = p_A + \delta u$ and $v = p_B + \delta v$. The per-locus heterozygosity of the cross, $u + v - 2uv$, expands to $$u + v - 2uv \;=\; \underbrace{p_A + p_B - 2p_Ap_B}_{\text{mean}} \;+\; \underbrace{(1 - 2p_B)\,\delta u}_{\text{parent A}} \;+\; \underbrace{(1 - 2p_A)\,\delta v}_{\text{parent B}} \;-\; \underbrace{2\,\delta u\, \delta v}_{\text{both}}$$ Four terms: one constant, one linear in each parent, one bilinear. Weight by $d_k$, sum over loci, and the classical decomposition falls out, $$H_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij}$$ with $$g^A_i = \sum_k d_k (1 - 2p_{Bk})\,\delta u_{ik}, \qquad s_{ij} = -2 \sum_k d_k\, \delta u_{ik}\, \delta v_{jk}$$ and $g^B_j$ symmetrically. What is linear in one parent is general combining ability: it is carried into every cross that parent enters. What is bilinear depends on *which two* lines met, and is specific combining ability. Because the deviations are taken from each pool's own line frequencies they sum to zero over that pool's lines, which is what makes the three components mean zero and mutually orthogonal. `heterosis_gca_sca()` is that expansion and nothing more: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} heterosis_gca_sca #> function (U, V, d) #> { #> stopifnot(ncol(U) == ncol(V), length(d) == ncol(U)) #> pA <- colMeans(U) #> pB <- colMeans(V) #> cU <- sweep(U, 2, pA) #> cV <- sweep(V, 2, pB) #> list(mu = heterosis_expected(pA, pB, d), gca_A = drop(cU %*% #> (d * (1 - 2 * pB))), gca_B = drop(cV %*% (d * (1 - 2 * #> pA))), sca = -2 * (cU * rep(d, each = nrow(U))) %*% t(cV)) #> } #> #> ``` ::: It reconstructs every hybrid in the factorial exactly, and all three components are mean zero: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cs <- heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d) H <- heterosis_value(ctx$X, d) ia <- ctx$ped$a ib <- ctx$ped$b - nA c(max_residual = max(abs(H - (cs$mu + cs$gca_A[ia] + cs$gca_B[ib] + cs$sca[cbind(ia, ib)]))), mu_vs_mean = abs(cs$mu - mean(H)), mean_gca_A = mean(cs$gca_A), mean_sca = mean(cs$sca)) #> max_residual mu_vs_mean mean_gca_A mean_sca #> 7.958079e-13 1.136868e-13 -4.796163e-16 -1.264766e-15 ``` ::: This is not a decomposition that resembles the two-way analysis of variance. It *is* the two-way analysis of variance: $\mu$, $g^A$ and $g^B$ are the grand mean and the row and column effects of the $H_{ij}$ table, and $s_{ij}$ is the interaction residual of the additive fit, to machine precision: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} max(abs(resid(lm(H ~ factor(ia) + factor(ib))) - cs$sca[cbind(ia, ib)])) #> [1] 6.966872e-12 ``` ::: @comstock1949 designed reciprocal recurrent selection around the distinction between these two components. The algebra above says what each one is made of -- and the next section says which of the two their scheme actually selects on. ### GCA is an average effect in the other pool's background Look at the weight on $\delta u$: it is $d_k(1 - 2p_{Bk})$, and $1 - 2p_B$ is $q_B - p_B$. That is the frequency factor of the classical average effect of a gene substitution, $a + d\,(q - p)$ [@falconer1996, Ch. 7], with two differences: the additive part $a$ is absent, because it belongs to the parental mean and not to $H$, and the frequencies are **pool B's**, not pool A's. This is the whole reason combining ability is not a property of a line. A pool-A line's alleles are always substituted into a pool-B background, so its general combining ability for heterosis is a dominance effect *evaluated at the tester pool's frequencies*. Change the tester pool and every number changes. Two limits follow immediately: - A locus at which the tester pool sits at $p_B = 0.5$ contributes **exactly zero** to $g^A$, whatever $\delta u_{ik}$ is. It still contributes to $g^B$, through $(1 - 2p_A)\,\delta v_{jk}$, and to $s_{ij}$; what it cannot do is discriminate between pool-A parents. - A locus at which the tester pool is fixed, $p_B \in \{0, 1\}$, has $\delta v \equiv 0$, so it contributes $\pm d_k\,\delta u_{ik}$ to $g^A$ and nothing to either $g^B$ or $s_{ij}$. The cross is then predictable from the pool-A parent by itself. Between those two limits sits every real programme, and @sec-heterosis-relocation is about which limit divergence pushes it towards. This is also the exact sense in which @comstock1949's scheme is built on the decomposition. Reciprocal recurrent selection evaluates each pool-A candidate on its cross performance against a *sample of the opposite pool*, and symmetrically for pool B. Averaging over testers removes $s_{ij}$, so of the heterosis in the decomposition above only $g^A_i$ survives as a contrast between pool-A candidates. Note what that does *not* say: cross performance is a genotypic value, not a mid-parent difference, so it also carries the candidate's own additive contribution -- the part that cancelled out of $H$ in the mid-parent derivation above and is not in this decomposition at all. Selection on testcross means therefore acts on the additive part and $g^A_i$ together. What the algebra here delimits is the dominance share of that response, and it says the share is general combining ability against the tester pool. ### SCA is minus twice a weighted parental inner product The bilinear term is $s_{ij} = -2\sum_k d_k\,\delta u_{ik}\,\delta v_{jk}$: minus twice the $d$-weighted inner product of the two parents' *centred* genotypes, a covariance up to the factor $1/m$. For $d_k > 0$, two parents that deviate from their pools in the same direction have a positive inner product and therefore a **negative** SCA. Read in words: two parents that resemble each other -- after removing what is typical of each pool -- cross badly, and the resemblance that counts is weighted by $d$, not by marker count. Similarity enters negatively throughout this chapter -- $1 - \theta_{AB}$, $d\,m\,(1 - f^L_{ab})$ -- but everywhere else it is similarity measured against a fixed base. Here it is measured against each pool's own mean, which is what makes the term specific to a *pair* rather than a property either parent carries into all its crosses. It is also @sec-heterosis-distance again. Since $\mu$, $g^A$ and $g^B$ are the grand, row and column means of the $H_{ij}$ table, $s_{ij}$ is the double-centred $H$ matrix. Under flat $d$, $H_{ij} = d\,m\,(1 - f^L_{ij})$, and double-centring annihilates the constant and flips the sign of what remains: $$s_{ij} \;=\; -\,d\,m \cdot \mathrm{DC}\big(f^L\big)_{ij},$$ with $\mathrm{DC}(M)_{ij} = M_{ij} - \bar M_{i\cdot} - \bar M_{\cdot j} + \bar M_{\cdot\cdot}$ over the $A \times B$ block. The factor $-dm$ is not cosmetic: $s_{ij}$ is on the trait scale and $f^L$ is a probability, and the minus is the same minus as in $-2\sum_k d_k \delta u\, \delta v$ -- more coancestry than the two margins predict means *less* SCA. So the coancestry kernel determines SCA under exactly the condition it determines heterosis, up to that constant, and stops doing so under exactly the same condition: a $d$ that varies across loci. ### The variance components Because the three components are orthogonal, the variance of heterosis over the factorial splits with them. Under the sampling model of the simulation -- each line's genotype an independent Bernoulli($p_{Ak}$) draw at every locus, so unrelated lines and linkage equilibrium within each pool -- each piece has a closed form in the pool frequencies: $$\sigma^2_{GCA_A} = \sum_k d_k^2\,(1 - 2p_{Bk})^2\,p_{Ak}q_{Ak}, \qquad \sigma^2_{SCA} = 4 \sum_k d_k^2\,p_{Ak}q_{Ak}\,p_{Bk}q_{Bk}$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} qa <- pA * (1 - pA) qb <- pB * (1 - pB) fmt(data.frame( component = c("GCA_A", "GCA_B", "SCA"), observed = c(var(cs$gca_A), var(cs$gca_B), var(as.vector(cs$sca))), closed_form = c(sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * pB)^2 * qa), sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * pA)^2 * qb), 4 * sum(d^2 * qa * qb))), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

The GCA rows are variances over 25 lines, whose relative sampling error is about $\sqrt{2/n} \approx$ 28%, and the agreement is within that. That error rate belongs to the independent-Bernoulli sampling model declared immediately above, not to the statistic: it is the sampling error of a variance over $n$ *independent* observations, and a recycled pool has no such $n$. @sec-heterosis-step7 measures how far the agreement moves once the lines are related. Note what each one requires. $\sigma^2_{SCA}$ carries $p_Aq_A\,p_Bq_B$: it needs **both** pools to be polymorphic. Fix either pool at a locus and that locus contributes no specific combining ability at all, whatever its $d_k$. Within-pool diversity is not merely something the diversity constraint defends; it is the raw material of SCA. ## Divergence destroys SCA faster than it builds GCA {#sec-heterosis-relocation} Put the two closed forms next to the drift argument of @sec-heterosis-flat and the variance tells a different story from the mean. The mean was flat; the variance is not, and it does not merely change shape. Under Balding-Nichols, $\mathbb{E}[p_Aq_A] = p(1-p)(1 - F_{ST})$ and $\mathbb{E}[(1 - 2p_B)^2] = (1-2p)^2 + 4F_{ST}\,p(1-p)$, and $p_A$ and $p_B$ are independent given the ancestral $p$. Per locus, in expectation over the draw, $$\mathbb{E}\big[\sigma^2_{SCA,k}\big] = 4d_k^2\,p^2(1-p)^2\,(1 - F_{ST})^2, \qquad \mathbb{E}\big[\sigma^2_{GCA_A,k}\big] = d_k^2\,p(1-p)\,(1 - F_{ST}) \left[(1-2p)^2 + 4F_{ST}\,p(1-p)\right]$$ Read the two expressions before reading the sweep, because they already say what it will show. Both carry the erosion factor $(1 - F_{ST})$, and both are **zero at $F_{ST} = 1$**: a pool fixed at every locus has no two lines that differ, so it has no combining-ability variance of either kind. Divergence therefore cannot transfer variance from one component to the other indefinitely; it destroys both in the limit. SCA carries the factor twice, because it needs both pools polymorphic at the same locus. GCA carries it once, multiplied by the tester factor $(1 - 2p_B)^2$, whose expectation *grows* with $F_{ST}$. The two expressions therefore behave differently in $F_{ST}$. The SCA expression is convex and decreasing on $[0, 1]$: it is a positive constant times $(1 - F_{ST})^2$, so it only ever falls. The GCA expression is a *concave* parabola, its $F_{ST}^2$ coefficient being $-4d_k^2p_k^2(1-p_k)^2$, and differentiating it gives the only turnover in this section. GCA variance rises from $F_{ST} = 0$ at a locus if and only if $8p(1-p) > 1$, that is $\tfrac12(1 - 1/\sqrt2) < p < \tfrac12(1 + 1/\sqrt2)$, and turns over at $$F^\star_k = \frac{8p_k(1-p_k) - 1}{8p_k(1-p_k)},$$ which is negative outside that interval -- at such loci GCA variance falls from the start. A sum of concave parabolas is a concave parabola, and its maximum works out to the $d_k^2\,(p_kq_k)^2$-weighted mean of the $F^\star_k$. Whether that mean lands inside $[0, 1]$ is a property of the ancestral frequency distribution, not a theorem: pools founded mostly at extreme frequencies would put it below zero and GCA variance would decline monotonically. Under the $U(0.05, 0.95)$ ancestral draw used here enough loci sit in the interval to place it inside the range, which is why the sweep below straddles a peak. The sweep's grid can show that the peak is interior; it cannot locate it. What is monotone is the ratio, $$\frac{\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_{SCA,k}]}{\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_{GCA_A,k}]} = \frac{4p(1-p)\,(1 - F_{ST})}{(1-2p)^2 + 4F_{ST}\,p(1-p)},$$ which falls in $F_{ST}$ at every locus. So the defensible statement is about the *share*, not about a transfer. Expected heterosis, we already know, does not move at all. Sweeping the pools apart -- same ancestral frequencies, fresh Balding-Nichols draws at each `fst`, as in @sec-heterosis-flat -- and evaluating the closed forms on the realised frequencies: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} reloc <- function(fst) { cf <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, seed = 5)) Pf <- pool_freqs(simulate_lines(cf) / 2, rep(c("A", "B"), c(cf$n_pool_A, cf$n_pool_B))) a <- Pf["A", ]; b <- Pf["B", ] va <- sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * b)^2 * a * (1 - a)) vb <- sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * a)^2 * b * (1 - b)) vs <- 4 * sum(d^2 * a * (1 - a) * b * (1 - b)) data.frame(fst = fst, var_GCA = va + vb, var_SCA = vs, frac_SCA = vs / (va + vb + vs)) } rl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45), reloc)) fmt(rl, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

The share result itself is not new in direction. @reif2007 prove that the ratio of dominance to additive variance in a hybrid population falls as its two parent populations diverge, and conclude that superior hybrids then become predictable from general combining ability effects. Their ratio is $\sigma^2_D / \sigma^2_A$ over the hybrid population, whose denominator contains the additive variance contributed by the parents -- the part that cancelled out of $H$ in the mid-parent derivation and is absent from everything computed here. This sharpens a question @sec-genomic-prediction had to leave open. That chapter fits one additive effect per marker and notes that such a model cannot represent SCA at all. The sweep says how large the unrepresentable share is, and how it moves: against poorly separated pools most of the variance in heterosis is specific; against well separated ones a minority is. These are shares of the variance in *heterosis*, not of total hybrid value, whose parental-mean part is additive at every $F_{ST}$. @technow2014 report high accuracy for additive hybrid prediction in established, clearly separated dent and flint pools, which is the regime where this model puts the specific share at its lowest -- consistent with the mechanism, though a single observational study in one crop cannot test it. :::: {.callout-warning} ## A smaller SCA share is not a better programme, and this is not a licence to maximise $F_{ST}$ Three things stay true at every point on that sweep. Expected heterosis does not change. The within-pool diversity spent to buy the divergence is spent for good. And $\sigma^2_{SCA} \to 0$ is the limit in which no cross is better than its parents predict -- there is nothing left to *find* by testing combinations, which is the activity the whole factorial exists to support. Past the peak of the GCA curve in @fig-heterosis-relocation even the predictable half shrinks: at $F_{ST} = 1$ there is no combining-ability variance of either kind, because no two lines in a pool differ. The falling SCA share is therefore a fact about what a predictor can express, not a gain. A programme reading it as one would be congratulating itself on having less to predict. So this is a second, independent reason for @sec-stages Trap 3's prescription to hold $F_{ST}$ in a band rather than at a maximum. @sec-heterosis-flat gave the diversity-side reason. This is the prediction-side one, and it points the same way. :::: ### What this says about ranking crosses The F1 of two fixed lines is genetically uniform, so the progeny-variance term that drives the usefulness criterion at @sec-stages S2 is zero for the hybrid itself, and cross ranking reduces to ranking means. That is true, and it is why this book ranks hybrids on an index rather than on $\mu + i h \sigma$. It does not follow that the ranking is easy. The *mean* of an F1 contains an SCA term that an additive $\mathbf{G}$ omits entirely, and @sec-heterosis-relocation sized its share of the variance in heterosis: a majority of it against weakly separated pools, a minority against well separated ones, and zero only at the degenerate limit where one pool is fixed at every locus. The progeny variance collapses; the dominance deviation does not. ## Running this on a real programme {#sec-heterosis-protocol} Eight steps, in the order they have to be executed on a maize-type programme's own data. Each one names the function to call, the quantity to check and what failure looks like. Steps 1-5 need only genotypes and pool labels. Steps 6-8 need more, and the requirement is worth naming because it is the reason these steps are rarely run. $H_{ij}$ is a **mid-parent difference**, so fitting the decomposition on real data needs the hybrid trial *and* per-se phenotypes of the parent lines, measured on the same scale as the hybrid trial: a separate inbred-level trial, in the same environments, with a common check set or an overlapping design to put the two on one scale. Very few programmes run one, because inbred per-se performance has no commercial value. Without it what the two-way layout of step 6 fits is hybrid *performance*, not heterosis, and its row effects are then general combining ability **plus** the parent's own additive contribution -- the term @sec-heterosis-gca-sca shows is not in $H$ at all. Both decompositions are legitimate; they are not the same decomposition, and the difference is exactly the parental additive part. ### Step 1 -- Verify the parents are inbred, and price it if they are not {#sec-heterosis-step1} Every formula in this chapter rests on the first premise. It is checkable in one line: an inbred line's self-coancestry is exactly 1, and its heterozygous fraction exactly 0. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c(min_self_coancestry = min(diag(molecular_coancestry(L / 2))), max_het_fraction = max(rowMeans(L / 2 == 0.5)), dominance_value_of_the_most_heterozygous_line = max(abs(heterosis_value(rbind(U, V), d)))) #> min_self_coancestry #> 1 #> max_het_fraction #> 0 #> dominance_value_of_the_most_heterozygous_line #> 0 ``` ::: If those numbers are not 1, 0 and 0, the parents are not fixed and the mid-parent already carries dominance of its own. The size of the resulting error is not small. Build parents that are *intra-pool* F1s instead of inbred lines -- one random cross within each pool, so each parent sits at its pool's random-mating heterozygosity -- then cross them across pools by drawing one gamete per parent per locus: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} intra_pool_f1 <- function(W, n, seed) { set.seed(seed) (W[sample.int(nrow(W), n, TRUE), ] + W[sample.int(nrow(W), n, TRUE), ]) / 2 } ZA <- intra_pool_f1(U, nrow(U), 101) ZB <- intra_pool_f1(V, nrow(V), 102) pd2 <- expand.grid(a = seq_len(nrow(ZA)), b = seq_len(nrow(ZB))) # One gamete per parent per locus, five independent draws of the whole factorial. draw <- t(vapply(1:5, function(r) { set.seed(200 + r) gA <- matrix(rbinom(length(ZA), 1, ZA), nrow(ZA))[pd2$a, ] gB <- matrix(rbinom(length(ZB), 1, ZB), nrow(ZB))[pd2$b, ] H <- heterosis_value((gA + gB) / 2, d) mp <- (heterosis_value(ZA, d)[pd2$a] + heterosis_value(ZB, d)[pd2$b]) / 2 c(hybrid_value = mean(H), mid_parent_gain = mean(H - mp)) }, numeric(2))) closed_form <- heterosis_expected(colMeans(ZA), colMeans(ZB), d) c(parent_het_fraction = mean(c(ZA, ZB) == 0.5), closed_form = closed_form, simulated_hybrid = mean(draw[, "hybrid_value"]), simulated_gain = mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"]), # The parental term is fixed across draws, so both columns carry the same s.d. sd_across_draws = sd(draw[, "hybrid_value"]), exact_sum_d_y2 = sum(d * (pA - pB)^2), overstatement = closed_form / mean(draw[, "mid_parent_gain"])) #> parent_het_fraction closed_form simulated_hybrid simulated_gain #> 0.294260 355.428354 355.106663 67.222488 #> sd_across_draws exact_sum_d_y2 overstatement #> 1.708396 65.890423 5.287343 ``` ::: Result. The parents carry 0.294 of their loci heterozygous. `heterosis_expected()` is still correct about the *hybrid*: it predicts 355.4 against a simulated 355.1 (s.d. 1.71 over five gamete draws), because that formula uses gamete frequencies only and does not care what the parents' own genotypes are. What it is not correct about is the *gain*: the mid-parent difference is 67.2, the same 1.71 standard deviation shifted down by the parents' own dominance value, so reading the closed form as heterosis overstates the gain by a factor of 5.29. The simulated gain agrees with the exact $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$ of @sec-heterosis-identity, 65.9, to within one standard deviation of the gamete draw. Interpretation, with its limit. The correction is not a fudge factor: it is the parents' own dominance contribution, 287.9 here, which `heterosis_value()` computes on the parent matrix directly and which is exactly zero under the inbred premise. Subtracting it recovers the mid-parent gain, and that gain matches the $\sum_k d_k y_k^2$ of @sec-heterosis-identity **in expectation only**: the realised intra-pool F1 parents are one draw, not their own expectation, so each replicate's mid-parent carries a sampling deviation of its own -- which is why the agreement reported above is to within one standard deviation of the gamete draw and not exact. The factor of 5.29 itself is specific to this configuration -- `fst` = 0.15, gamma-distributed $d$, parents at full random-mating heterozygosity -- and it shrinks toward 1 as the parents approach fixation. Five gamete draws at one seed family give the dispersion reported and no more. **Call.** `diag(molecular_coancestry(GL))`; `heterosis_value()` on the parent matrix, not only on the hybrids. **Check.** Self-coancestry 1 and heterozygous fraction 0 for every parent. **Warning sign.** Any parent with a heterozygous fraction above the marker error rate. Partially inbred parents (S1, S2, clonal maintenance of a heterozygous plant) invalidate the mid-parent cancellation, not the hybrid prediction. **Threshold.** `heterosis_value()` on the parent set must return zero to machine precision. If it does not, subtract it: the mid-parent gain is the hybrid value minus the parents' mean, always. ### Step 2 -- Compute pool frequencies, and keep them distinct from $p_0$ {#sec-heterosis-step2} `pool_freqs(GL, pool)` returns one row per pool. These are the *current* cycle's frequencies and they are supposed to move; they are not the frozen base $p_0$ that @sec-genomic-era's two inbreeding lenses are measured against. Both objects are frequency vectors over the same markers and confusing them produces a heterosis prediction anchored to a population that no longer exists. **Call.** `pool_freqs(GL / 2, pool)` on the current cycle's line matrix. **Check.** `nrow() == 2` and the pool labels are the heterotic groups, not families or locations. **Warning sign.** A pool frequency vector computed over *hybrids* rather than lines. On the full factorial that gives $(p_A + p_B)/2$ for both pools -- @sec-era-step1 proves the identity -- which sets $y \equiv 0$ and reports the divergence term as zero. **Threshold.** None; this is a bookkeeping step, and the only failure is silent. ### Step 3 -- Decide what stands in for $d_k$, and say so {#sec-heterosis-step3} Nothing below step 4 can be computed without a weight per locus. Three defensible choices, in decreasing order of what they require: 1. **Estimated $d_k$** from a dominance model fitted on hybrid data. This is what the third premise assumes exists, and it is the only option that lets $\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$ be computed. 2. **Flat $d_k \equiv 1$**, which makes $H$ proportional to marker distance and the whole calculation a function of the coancestry kernel (@sec-heterosis-distance). Everything in this chapter's frequency algebra still holds; what is lost is alignment, which is exactly the term flat $d$ sets to zero. 3. **No $d$ at all**, reporting only $GD_{BS}$ and `mean_sq_delta_p`, which is the frequency half of the divergence term and is exact (@sec-heterosis-alignment says what is missing). The cost of choice 2 is measurable, and it is the correlation already computed in @sec-heterosis-distance: under flat $d$ heterosis and marker distance are the same statistic, and under the gamma-distributed $d$ used here the correlation between them is 0.78. **Call.** `heterosis_value(X, d)` with whichever vector you have chosen, and record the choice next to the number. **Check.** `length(d) == ncol(X)` and $d$ indexed in the same marker order. **Warning sign.** A report that gives expected heterosis without saying which of the three choices produced it. At the correlation just quoted the choices are not interchangeable for ranking crosses, and their absolute values are on different scales altogether. **Threshold.** If choice 2 is used, state that alignment is assumed zero, because that is what flat $d$ asserts. ### Step 4 -- Partition, and cross-check against the diversity partition {#sec-heterosis-step4} `heterosis_partition(pA, pB, d)` returns `shared`, `divergence` and `total`. With $d \equiv 1$ and divided by $m$ the first two are the $GD_T$ and $GD_{BS}$ of `gd_partition()`, and the chunk in @sec-heterosis-identity checks that to twelve digits. Running both is a consistency test worth the two lines it costs -- but only if the two calls are given the **same line weights**, and by default they are not. The algebra says why. For any weights $w$ over the lines of a pool, with inbred lines, $\theta_A = \overline{p_{A,w}^2 + q_{A,w}^2}$ where $p_{A,w} = \sum_i w_i u_{ik}$ is the *weighted* pool frequency, and the same for $B$ and for $\theta_{AB}$. Substituting into `gd_partition()`'s definitions, $GD_T = 1 - \bar f = \overline{2\bar p(1 - \bar p)}$ and $GD_{BS} = \tilde f - \bar f = \overline{(p_{A,w} - p_{B,w})^2}/2$, which are exactly `heterosis_partition()`'s two terms evaluated at $p_{A,w}$ and $p_{B,w}$. So the identity holds for *any* weighting -- as long as both sides use the same one. `gd_partition(idx, ctx)` weights each line by how often the selection uses it (`line_weights()`), while `pool_freqs()` is unweighted. On the full factorial usage is uniform and the two coincide; on a selected subset they do not, and the discrepancy is not small: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} i_trunc <- sel_truncation(ctx, 60) # index truncation: deliberately unbalanced gp_sel <- gd_partition(i_trunc, ctx) GLh <- L / 2 wt <- line_weights(i_trunc, ctx) hp2 <- function(a, b) { heterosis_partition(a, b, rep(1, ctx$m))[c("shared", "divergence")] / ctx$m } cmp <- rbind( `all lines, unweighted` = hp2(pA, pB), `lines used, unweighted` = hp2(colMeans(GLh[unique(ctx$ped$a[i_trunc]), ]), colMeans(GLh[unique(ctx$ped$b[i_trunc]), ])), `usage-weighted` = hp2(as.vector(wt[["A"]] %*% GLh), as.vector(wt[["B"]] %*% GLh)), `gd_partition(idx, ctx)` = c(gp_sel[["GD_T"]], gp_sel[["GD_BS"]])) stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(cmp["usage-weighted", ]), c(gp_sel[["GD_T"]], gp_sel[["GD_BS"]])))) fmt(data.frame(cmp, shared_err_pct = 100 * (cmp[, "shared"] / gp_sel[["GD_T"]] - 1), divergence_err_pct = 100 * (cmp[, "divergence"] / gp_sel[["GD_BS"]] - 1)), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

With usage weights on both sides the identity is exact to machine precision -- the `stopifnot()` enforces it -- while the unweighted pool frequencies of `pool_freqs()` overstate `shared` by +5.0% and understate `divergence` by 35.9% on this 60-hybrid truncation set, which uses only 10 pool-A lines with one of them in 23 of the 60 crosses. Restricting the unweighted mean to the lines actually used recovers part of the gap and not the rest, because the usage *within* the used set is itself far from uniform. Interpretation. The two functions are not inconsistent; they answer the same question on two different populations -- a notional pool in which every line is equally represented, and the pool as the selection actually weights it. Which one a report wants depends on the question, and the only error is comparing one with the other and calling the difference a bug. The order of magnitude quoted here is one selection at one scale; a plan with a usage cap (`max_use`) sits between the two rows. **Call.** `heterosis_partition()` on the pool frequencies and `gd_partition(idx, ctx)` on the hybrid set -- with the pool frequencies weighted by `line_weights(idx, ctx)` if the two are to be compared at all. **Check.** `shared / m == GD_T` and `divergence / m == GD_BS` under flat $d$, **both computed from usage-weighted pool frequencies**. On the full factorial, or under any uniform usage, the unweighted `pool_freqs()` satisfies this too. **Warning sign.** A disagreement on a selected subset is almost always the weighting above, not a coding error: check `line_weights()` first, and only then whether the lines are coded 0/1 or the pool labels differ between the calls. A $GD_{WI}$ that is not zero is the separate failure -- with inbred parents it must be, and a non-zero value means the line matrix contains heterozygotes, back to step 1. **Threshold.** Machine precision when both sides carry the same weights. With unweighted pool frequencies against a selected subset, expect tens of per cent on the divergence term, of the size measured above, and do not treat it as a tolerance to tighten. ### Step 5 -- Log `mean_sq_delta_p` every cycle {#sec-heterosis-step5} `s1_monitor(GL / 2, pool, cycle)` is the per-cycle panel. Of its three divergence columns only `mean_sq_delta_p` is exact -- it is $\overline{y^2}$, so half of it is $GD_{BS}$ -- and `frac_opposite_fixed` is zero across most of the useful range, as the sweep in @sec-heterosis-flat shows. **Call.** `s1_monitor()` once per cycle, appended to a single data frame. **Check.** `mean_sq_delta_p / 2` against `gd_partition()`'s `GD_BS`. **Warning sign.** `frac_opposite_fixed` used as the divergence statistic. In the sweep of @sec-heterosis-flat it is exactly zero at every `fst` up to 0.10 -- not one marker in 2000 -- while over the same span the divergence term has already risen by a factor of 2.3 (0.0107 to 0.0246 per locus at $d = 1$). The first non-zero entry is at `fst` = 0.2, by which point divergence has risen 4.1-fold. **Threshold.** A *band* on $F_{ST}$, not a maximum. @sec-heterosis-flat gives the diversity-side reason and @sec-heterosis-relocation the prediction-side one. ### Step 6 -- Check that the crossing layout identifies what you intend to fit {#sec-heterosis-step6} This is the step most often skipped, and it is arithmetic, not opinion. The decomposition $H_{ij} = \mu + g^A_i + g^B_j + s_{ij}$ is the two-way layout with identified rows and columns. Averaging a pool-A line over $k$ testers leaves it with $g^A_i$ plus the mean of $k$ specific deviations, so the correlation between the testcross mean and the true $g^A$ is $$r_k = \left[1 + \frac{\sigma^2_{SCA}}{\sigma^2_{GCA_A}} \cdot \frac{n_B - k}{k\,(n_B - 1)}\right]^{-1/2}$$ where the second factor is the finite-population correction for drawing $k$ of the $n_B$ available testers without replacement; at $k = n_B$ it vanishes and $r_k = 1$ exactly, because the row mean of the complete factorial *is* $\mu + g^A_i$. ::: ::: Result. A single tester ranks pool-A lines for general combining ability with a correlation of 0.49 (s.d. 0.12 over 20 tester choices); five testers give 0.85 and ten give 0.94. No $k$ deviates from the closed form by as much as one standard deviation of the tester-set spread: the two largest residuals are $k = 1$ at -0.5 s.d. and $k = 3$ at 0.6 s.d., in opposite directions, and $k = 3$ is the larger of the two. Singling out $k = 1$ would be reading the *absolute* gap (0.066, the largest in the table) while ignoring that $k = 1$ also has by far the largest dispersion by construction -- one tester, one draw of $s_{ij}$, nothing averaged. Measured against the standard error of a 20-replicate mean rather than against the single-draw spread, both residuals are larger than the noise (-2.4 and 2.6 standard errors), so the closed form is not exact at small $k$ and this section does not claim it is. Two reasons are identifiable and neither is modelled here: $r_k$ is a function of an *expected* sampling variance, whereas the table averages 20 correlations, and $x \mapsto (1 + x)^{-1/2}$ is convex, so the two are not the same quantity; and $\mathrm{cov}_i(g^A_i, \overline{s}_{i\cdot})$ vanishes only when the mean runs over all $n_B$ testers, not over a subset. The scan is reported as a measurement with its dispersion, not as a validated formula. Interpretation. The whole scan is driven by one ratio, $\sigma^2_{SCA}/\sigma^2_{GCA_A} =$ 2.2 here. That ratio is what @sec-heterosis-relocation shows falling as the pools diverge, so the number of testers a programme needs is not a constant of the crop: well separated pools need fewer. Two limits. This is heterosis only -- the parental additive contribution to testcross performance is not in $H$ and is not tested here -- and it is one realisation of $d$ and one pool pair, so the ratio, and with it every entry in the table, moves with the seed. **Call.** `qr(model.matrix(...))$rank` on the layout you actually have, before fitting anything; `heterosis_gca_sca()` only once the layout supports it. **Check.** `sca_df > 0` if SCA is to be estimated; `residual_df > 0` if it is to be tested. **Warning sign.** A testcross file against one inbred tester per pool, analysed as though it estimated SCA. It estimates $\mu + g^A_i + (\text{that tester's contribution})$ and nothing else. **Threshold.** Two testers to identify SCA; from the scan above, five to ten to rank GCA at $r > 0.85$ at this $\sigma^2_{SCA}/\sigma^2_{GCA}$ ratio -- and recompute the requirement when the ratio changes. ### Step 7 -- Fit the decomposition and check it reconstructs {#sec-heterosis-step7} `heterosis_gca_sca(U, V, d)` is the expansion, not a model fit: it needs no solver and returns $\mu$, `gca_A`, `gca_B` and the `sca` matrix. On simulated $d$ it must reconstruct every hybrid exactly, and the chunk in @sec-heterosis-gca-sca asserts that together with the `lm()` interaction equivalence. On real data $d$ is unknown, so the route reverses: fit `lm(H ~ factor(a) + factor(b))`, take the row and column effects as $g^A$ and $g^B$ and the residual as $s_{ij}$. The two routes coincide only on a complete, balanced factorial. **Call.** `heterosis_gca_sca()` when $d$ is known (simulation); `lm()` with both parent factors when it is not. **Check.** The reconstruction residual, and that all three components are mean zero. **Warning sign.** A non-zero mean for `gca_A` or `sca`. The deviations are taken from each pool's own line frequencies, so they sum to zero over that pool by construction; a non-zero mean means the frequencies used were not the pool's. **Threshold.** Machine precision for the reconstruction. **For the variance components there is no threshold that transfers to a real pool**, and the $\sqrt{2/n}$ figure quoted in @sec-heterosis-gca-sca is not one. That tolerance is the relative sampling error of a variance over $n$ **independent** observations, and it is valid there only because the closed forms are derived under the simulation's sampling model -- each line's genotype an independent Bernoulli($p_k$) draw at every locus, hence unrelated lines and linkage equilibrium within pool. A recycled heterotic pool satisfies neither: assumption A3 of @sec-era-programme makes within-pool recycling the normal state of this system, so its lines share ancestors. The size of the failure can be measured, at least for the relatedness half of it. Re-derive each pool as 25 doubled haploids drawn from crosses among six of its own members -- one Bernoulli draw per locus, so the lines are **related but carry no linkage disequilibrium** -- and compare the closed forms with the observed variances on five such pairs of pools: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rel_dev <- function(A, B) { # % deviation, observed vs closed form p1 <- colMeans(A); p2 <- colMeans(B) cc <- heterosis_gca_sca(A, B, d) obs <- c(var(cc$gca_A), var(cc$gca_B), var(as.vector(cc$sca))) cf <- c(sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * p2)^2 * p1 * (1 - p1)), sum(d^2 * (1 - 2 * p1)^2 * p2 * (1 - p2)), 4 * sum(d^2 * p1 * (1 - p1) * p2 * (1 - p2))) 100 * (obs / cf - 1) } recycle <- function(W, n_found) { # DH lines from crosses among founders fo <- W[sample.int(nrow(W), n_found), , drop = FALSE] t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(W)), function(i) { pr <- sample.int(n_found, 2) rbinom(ncol(W), 1, (fo[pr[1], ] + fo[pr[2], ]) / 2) }, numeric(ncol(W)))) } dev <- t(vapply(1:5, function(r) { set.seed(500 + r) # seeded per draw, not once rel_dev(recycle(U, 6), recycle(V, 6)) }, numeric(3))) dimnames(dev) <- list(paste0("draw", 1:5), c("GCA_A", "GCA_B", "SCA")) fmt(rbind(dev, `independent lines` = rel_dev(U, V)), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}

On the five recycled pairs 5 of the 15 components fall outside that band and the largest deviation is 56%. The two GCA columns carry almost all of it; the SCA column stays within 10.3%. Interpretation, and its limits. A variance of a sum over loci picks up the between-line covariance that relatedness induces, which the closed forms -- being sums of per-locus terms -- do not contain; the GCA components are sums over loci weighted by the tester pool's frequencies and are the ones exposed. This says the tolerance must be recalibrated empirically on the programme's own pedigree, not that the closed forms are wrong: they remain exact statements about the sampling model they are derived under. The construction here is a caricature (six founders, one DH per F1, five draws, one seed family) and it isolates *relatedness only* -- there is no linkage disequilibrium in it, because each locus is drawn independently. A real recycled pool violates the sampling model on both counts at once, and the size of the linkage contribution is not measured anywhere in this book. ### Step 8 -- Decide the $F_{ST}$ band on alignment, not on $F_{ST}$ {#sec-heterosis-step8} The output of steps 4-7 answers one management question: should the pools be pushed further apart? The chapter's answer is that $F_{ST}$ cannot inform it (@sec-heterosis-flat: the total does not move) and that the quantity that can is $\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$ (@sec-heterosis-alignment: a factor of 1.55 at constant $F_{ST}$). **Call.** $\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$ with the population divisor, alongside $\bar d\,\overline{y^2}$; the two-term identity of @sec-heterosis-alignment is the check. **Check.** The sign and magnitude of the covariance relative to $\bar d\,\overline{y^2}$. **Warning sign.** A proposal to raise $F_{ST}$ justified by the divergence term alone. Under neutral divergence the shared term pays for all of it, unit for unit, and $\sigma^2_{SCA}$ falls at the same time. **Threshold.** No universal one exists, and this chapter does not supply it: the missing weight $\lambda$ between within- and between-pool diversity needs the two covariances listed in @sec-heterosis-lambda, and this book estimates neither. ## What this does not change :::: {.callout-warning} ## The diversity constraint stays additive Nothing in this chapter reopens the optimisation. $\theta$, $GD$ and $\alpha$ are computed on molecular coancestry and are functions of the frequencies alone; no dominance term enters them, and @sec-ocs, @sec-combinatorial and @sec-advanced are untouched. The combining-ability split of @sec-heterosis-gca-sca sits outside the constraint for the same reason: it is a statement about the objective, not about the feasible set. A dominance model changes the **mean-performance ranking**, not the diversity term. @sec-case-study states the same separation from the other side. Do not conflate them, and do not read this chapter as licence to put a heterosis term inside the constraint. :::: What it does change is the interpretation of the constraint's output. Two plans with the same $\alpha$ and the same $GD_{BS}$ can differ in expected heterosis by half again, if one of them concentrated its divergence on the dominance loci -- that is the scenario table of @sec-heterosis-alignment, whose three columns share every frequency-based statistic. The partition cannot distinguish them. Only an estimate of $d$ can. ### What it would take to use $d$ {#sec-heterosis-lambda} @sec-catalogue leaves a weight $\lambda$ undetermined between within- and between-pool diversity and observes that the ratio of the two heterosis terms is what $\lambda$ is trying to express. This chapter can now say what would have to be estimated to set it, and it is not much: - **$\lambda$ needs two covariances, not $d$ itself.** Each heterosis term is $m$ times a mean times a mean plus a covariance, so their ratio needs $\mathrm{cov}(d, y^2)$ and $\mathrm{cov}(d, 2\bar p(1 - \bar p))$, each relative to $\bar d$, on top of what the frequencies already give. A programme does not need per-locus dominance deviations to weight the two diversity terms against each other; it needs to know whether its divergence is landing on its dominance loci. - **Ranking crosses needs more.** $s_{ij}$ is a $d$-weighted inner product between two specific parents, so it needs the deviations locus by locus. This is the extension @sec-case-study names and the book does not attempt. - **Fitting it needs a factorial, and a testcross file is not one.** The decomposition above is the two-way layout with *identified* rows and columns: each pool-A line crossed to several named pool-B lines and each pool-B line to several named pool-A lines, which is what makes $g^A$, $g^B$ and $s_{ij}$ separately estimable and what the `lm()` above fits. Testcrosses against a single common tester give only a column of $\mu + g^A_i + \text{(one tester's contribution)}$ -- no SCA is identifiable, because there is no second tester to contrast against. Programmes that already cross two pools in a partial factorial for hybrid evaluation have the layout; programmes that testcross against one inbred tester per pool do not. ## Where this connects @sec-subdivided supplied the partition and @sec-catalogue will use it; this chapter supplies the reason the $GD_{BS}$ component is singled out for protection, and the reason protecting it is not the same as maximising it. @sec-stages Trap 3 already recommended holding $F_{ST}$ in a band: @sec-heterosis-flat is why a band, and @sec-heterosis-alignment is what to watch instead of the band. @sec-heterosis-distance closes the loop with the coancestry kernel of @sec-coancestry: under flat dominance, the diversity matrix and the heterosis prediction are the same object. @sec-genomic-prediction is the chapter this one supplies a missing term to. It predicts breeding values with an additive model on a trait that is additive by construction, and lists specific combining ability first among what it does not model. @sec-heterosis-gca-sca is where that term comes from and @sec-heterosis-relocation is what share of the variance in heterosis it holds; both are derived here rather than fitted, because on a simulated $d$ they can be. It also gives a reason why a heterotic *pattern* -- which pool crosses well onto which -- is not recoverable from how far apart the pools have drifted: @sec-heterosis-alignment's three scenarios share every frequency-based statistic and differ by half again in expected heterosis. @white2020 describe heterotic patterns and diversity separately in North American proprietary dent germplasm; this chapter says why the two need describing separately. Forward, the alignment result is the argument for @sec-cycles. Drift moves frequencies independently of $d$, and selection on a line's own performance cannot respond to $d$ either, because an inbred line's dominance contribution is exactly zero (@sec-heterosis-id) -- which leaves selection on *cross* performance as the only process in this model that can move frequencies in a way that depends on where the dominance is. The alignment between divergence and dominance is therefore something each cycle either builds or erodes, not a standing asset. A one-cycle constraint cannot see that, and neither can $F_{ST}$. @sec-alphasimr runs that loop on a dominance trait and is the pipeline this chapter's algebra describes.
